definition: Cadence means a rhythm or progression of sound.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word cadence. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know cadence should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: You could set a watch by the auctioneer's cadence, numbers rising and dipping in the same rolling pattern all afternoon.
A monotone is the bare opposite of a cadence — every syllable on the same flat note, nothing rising, nothing falling, no pattern for a listener to ride.
A lilt stops short of a full cadence — a hint of music in a voice, pleasant but loose, without the steady repeating pattern a drummer could follow.

Rhythm is the everyday, catch-all word for any repeating beat — a heartbeat, rain on a roof, a drum loop. A cadence is a more particular rhythm: the patterned rise and fall of a voice or a movement, a shape you could march to. Every cadence is a rhythm; most rhythms are not cadences.

Tempo is only the speed of the music — how fast the beats come, something you could state as a number. A cadence is the shape of the pattern itself, the rise and fall a listener can ride. Doubling the tempo makes the waltz faster; it is still the same cadence.

Meter is the counted, formal grid of beats — four beats to a bar, five stresses to a line — the kind of pattern you write down and check. A cadence is the living pattern you hear, rising and falling as it moves. Meter is the ruled paper; cadence is the handwriting.

A cascade is the root made visible — water falling ledge to ledge in one continuous spill.
Cadence means a rhythm or progression of sound.

Double-dutch turners at the rec center keep a cadence you can hear from the parking lot — two slaps and a skip, two slaps and a skip — and the girls time their jumps to it without ever looking down at the ropes.
Cadence is the word because it means a rhythm or progression of sound — the slap-slap-skip repeats like a drummed sentence, and everything else organizes itself around that shape.
Tempo would name only the speed; cadence names the rise and fall a body can ride.
Cadence is for the pattern in sound or motion — speech, drumming, rowing, marching.
If only speed is at issue, tempo; if only the tune, melody.
Reach for cadence when you can feel where the next beat will land.

Recruits at Fort Barrow learn the base's history from a plaque, but they learn its sound from Sergeant Odom.
Her marching count is famous: a call that climbs, hangs a beat, then drops as the boots strike — the same rising-and-falling shape at dawn as at dusk.
New recruits fight it, trying to march by counting alone.
Veterans stop counting and simply ride it.
One graduate, asked years later what he remembered of Fort Barrow, did not mention the drills.
He hummed Odom's cadence — climb, hang, fall — and his whole table hummed it back.
The words of the count change every season.
The shape of it never has.
